scene: A Cynic has taken up residence in a jar by the harbor and is telling your students that your school is a shop.

choices.label: Debate him in front of the jar
choices.resultText: He wins, in the sense that he has nothing to lose. You win, in the sense that your students come back the next morning.

choices.label: Bring him bread and sit with him
choices.resultText: He eats, insults you thoughtfully, and admits the jar is cold. Your students see you sit in the dust. It is better teaching than the lecture.

scene: A letter from the Museum at Alexandria: they have heard of your work and would house you for a year among the scrolls. The salary is royal. So is the leash.

choices.label: Go for the year
choices.resultText: The Library, Euclid's students, and a king who reads what you write. You come home with a chest of copies and a habit of looking over your shoulder.

choices.label: Stay; Massalia is where your questions are
choices.resultText: The letter is framed by your students, who tell it at every symposium. Alexandria writes to someone else.

scene: Three students owe a season's fees. One is a Kleitos, one a fisherman's son, one a Gaulish chief's boy learning Greek.

choices.label: Forgive the fisherman's son, bill the others
choices.resultText: The Kleitos pays, the chief pays in a horse, the fisherman's son pays in fish for the rest of your life.

choices.label: Bill them all, equally
choices.resultText: All three pay. The fisherman's son does not come back. He was the one asking the good questions.

scene: You have calculated an eclipse for the day after tomorrow, using a Babylonian table a trader sold you. Announce it and be either a prophet or a fool.

choices.label: Announce it in the agora
choices.resultText: The sun goes dark on schedule. The priests are furious. The fishmongers now ask you about the weather.

choices.label: Tell your students only
choices.resultText: The sun goes dark. Your students are speechless. One of them tells the priests, who are furious anyway, more quietly.

scene: A Gaulish wise-man, some say druid, has heard of you and proposes a debate at the western gate on whether the soul dies. He speaks Greek. Badly, and well.

choices.label: Meet him at the gate
choices.resultText: He believes the soul passes into another body. You believe you do not know. The crowd prefers his answer and your argument.

choices.label: Refuse; philosophy is Greek
choices.resultText: He debates a Dynatoi sophist instead. The sophist loses. You are told this by everyone.

scene: A magistrate whose son quoted you at dinner has laid a charge: corrupting the young. It has been done before, to better men.

choices.label: Defend yourself in the assembly, as Socrates did not
choices.resultText: You are acquitted by twelve votes and quoted by twelve hundred. The son now quotes you more.

choices.label: Apologize and pay a fine
choices.resultText: The charge is withdrawn. The son stops quoting you. Your students notice which of Socrates' choices you did not make.

scene: A citizen's daughter has been listening at the door of the stoa for a month. She asks to sit inside. Her father does not know.

choices.label: Admit her
choices.resultText: She is better than the boys. Her father finds out, rages, and then quietly asks what she has learned.

choices.label: Let her keep the door
choices.resultText: She listens at the door for a year, and then marries. Her son, later, is your best student, and asks who taught his mother.

scene: A sophist in Syracuse is teaching your treatise as his own, with your best argument and his worse conclusion.

choices.label: Write to Syracuse and expose him
choices.resultText: Your letter is read at his school. He leaves Syracuse. The treatise, now famous for being stolen, sells.

choices.label: Let ideas travel; they were never yours
choices.resultText: He teaches it for years. Some of his students find the original. The original is better, and they say so.

scene: The Saluvian hostage-boys in the council house need a philosopher, the Archons say, to learn what a polis is. The fee is civic, which means small.

choices.label: Teach them
choices.resultText: They learn what a polis is and ask, reasonably, why theirs is not one. You have no good answer. That is the lesson.

choices.label: Decline; hostages do not need Plato
choices.resultText: A sophist teaches them rhetoric instead. They go home able to argue, and do.

scene: A follower of Pyrrho arrives, suspends judgment on everything, and is winning your students by refusing to argue with them.

choices.label: Engage him on his own ground
choices.resultText: You cannot refute a man who asserts nothing. You learn a great deal trying, and so, watching, do your students.

choices.label: Mock him at the symposium
choices.resultText: The mockery is good and the wine is better. He suspends judgment on both, and keeps your students another month.

scene: The Archon offers you a place at his shoulder as adviser: real influence, and every conclusion read by a man who needs it to be useful.

choices.label: Accept the place
choices.resultText: Your advice shapes a treaty and a tariff. Your treatise waits. Your students learn that philosophy has an office.

choices.label: Refuse; a philosopher advises the city from the stoa
choices.resultText: He takes a sophist instead. The tariff is worse. You say so from the stoa, which is exactly where you said you would.

scene: A student brings you a scroll of Theophrastus on plants, with the passage on poisons marked, heavily, by a previous owner.

choices.label: Study the botany, skip the mark
choices.resultText: Plants of the East, and their virtues. You copy the useful parts. The marked passage you leave unmarked in your copy.

choices.label: Burn the marked page
choices.resultText: One page of Theophrastus in the brazier. The student is scandalized. The scroll is less complete and, you decide, more useful.

scene: The tyrant of Syracuse invites philosophers to his court. Plato went, twice, and it went badly twice. The stipend is large.

choices.label: Go, and keep your mouth judicious
choices.resultText: Marble, flattery, a ruler who wants to be told he is wise. You are, judiciously. You come home with the stipend and a taste in your mouth.

choices.label: Refuse, and cite Plato
choices.resultText: Your refusal is quoted in Syracuse, where a sophist takes the stipend and is very well fed.

scene: A rich patron wants a floor mosaic of the five regular solids for his andron, and wants you to explain them to his guests at the unveiling.

choices.label: Explain them, and take the fee
choices.resultText: Twenty drunk men learn the dodecahedron. Two of them remember it. One of them sends his son to your school.

choices.label: Decline; geometry is not a dinner act
choices.resultText: A sophist explains them, wrong. The mosaic is beautiful. You go to look at it when the patron is out.

scene: A letter from Strato at the Lyceum asks for your observations on the tides at the Ocean's edge, for a treatise on the moon. Pytheas's numbers are in your chest.

choices.label: Copy them and send them
choices.resultText: Your name in an Athenian treatise, in a footnote, forever. Your students find the footnote and behave as if it were a statue.

choices.label: Keep them for your own work
choices.resultText: The treatise appears without your numbers, wrong about the tides. You are right, in a drawer.

scene: A household slave, sent to fetch you, has been standing at the stoa's edge for a month, listening. He reads. He asks, once, quietly, if he may sit.

choices.label: Let him sit
choices.resultText: He sits. Two citizens leave. The rest stay, and the slave asks a question about justice that none of them can answer.

choices.label: Tell him the stoa is for citizens
choices.resultText: He goes. He keeps standing at the edge. You keep noticing.

scene: Your library, forty scrolls, would fetch a fortune from a Rhodian collector. You have read them all. Your students have read none.

choices.label: Sell them
choices.resultText: Forty scrolls sail to Rhodes. You have the silver and the memory. Your students have your memory.

choices.label: Open them to your students
choices.resultText: Scrolls come back stained with oil and argument. One does not come back at all, which is what libraries are for.

scene: You have designed a water-clock for the agora that keeps the hours through the night. The city will fund it if you present it in person, to men who will ask about the cost.

choices.label: Present it
choices.resultText: The clock runs. Merchants argue with it. It is called your clock even after it is replaced.

choices.label: Send the plans and let an engineer present
choices.resultText: The clock runs. It is called the engineer's clock. You are paid for the plans, which you wanted less than you thought.

scene: Your treatise is ready. Copying it for the wider Greek world means scribes and papyrus and a season's silver.

choices.label: Pay for ten copies
choices.resultText: Ten copies, to Athens, Syracuse, Rhodes, Alexandria. Two are argued with in writing. That is fame.

choices.label: One copy, for the stoa
choices.resultText: One copy, read by your students, argued with in person. That is teaching.

scene: A shipping House will pay very well for a speech proving that a contract they broke was never binding. You could prove it. You could prove the opposite by noon.

choices.label: Take the fee and win the case
choices.resultText: You win. The contract was never binding, now. Your students learn what an argument can do, and some of them are frightened.

choices.label: Refuse; truth is not a brief
choices.resultText: They hire a Syracusan who wins it worse. You are poorer and your students are not frightened.

scene: A magistrate sits in your stoa, in state, and asks you to define justice for the benefit of the crowd. He expects a compliment.

choices.label: Question him until the crowd sees him squirm
choices.resultText: He leaves without his definition. The crowd has learned what a definition is. He has learned what a philosopher is, and does not forgive it.

choices.label: Give him a definition he can quote
choices.resultText: He quotes it for a year. It is wrong. You are the only one who minds.

scene: The old wool-warehouse by the stoa is for sale. With a roof and a name it would be a school, yours, with students who pay and a legacy that compounds.

choices.label: Buy it and found the school
choices.resultText: A roof, a name over the door, and thirty students by autumn. The name over the door is yours, and it outlasts the roof.

choices.label: The stoa was good enough for Zeno
choices.resultText: The stoa. The rain. Zeno. Your students bring cloaks.

scene: A Roman envoy, a plain man with Greek learned from a slave, asks you what philosophy is for. He seems to want a practical answer.

choices.label: Give him an afternoon
choices.resultText: He listens to the Stoics longest. He asks about duty and cost. You suspect Rome will take what it needs from Greece and leave the rest.

choices.label: Tell him it is not for anything
choices.resultText: He nods, writes something down, and leaves. You wonder for years what he wrote.

scene: Timaeus the historian, in exile from Sicily, writes asking for the true story of Protis and Gyptis, which every Massaliote knows and no two tell the same.

choices.label: Research it properly and send what you find
choices.resultText: Three versions, one stone, and a Ligurian song. He uses all of it. Massalia is in his history the way you wrote it.

choices.label: Send him the version the city likes
choices.resultText: He uses it. It is beautiful and not quite true. The city is very pleased with its history.

scene: Two of your students, having read the Stoics too young, announce they will leave the city to live as sages on a rock in the gulf, eating shellfish.

choices.label: Go with them for a week
choices.resultText: A week of shellfish and stars. They come home cured of rocks and full of questions. So, oddly, are you.

choices.label: Forbid it and write to their fathers
choices.resultText: They stay. They resent it. One of them, at forty, goes to a rock anyway, and writes to thank you for the delay.

scene: A patron who promised a fee for a lecture on the gods now says he expected a lecture on the gods, not on whether there are any.

choices.label: Take him before the magistrates
choices.resultText: The magistrates listen to both the lecture and the complaint. They pay you and fine you. Net, you are ahead, and famous.

choices.label: Forgive the fee and keep the argument
choices.resultText: He tells everyone he cheated a philosopher. Everyone knows what a philosopher he cheated said. You lose a fee and win the season.

scene: A young astronomer from Samos, passing through, argues over wine that the earth goes round the sun. He is very drunk and, you are nearly sure, right.

choices.label: Sit up all night and check his numbers
choices.resultText: By dawn you believe him and cannot prove it. Neither can he. You write it down anyway, in case.

choices.label: Send him to bed
choices.resultText: He sails in the morning. Years later a scroll from Samos makes you put down your cup.

scene: A deposed Sicilian tyrant, living quietly in the upper city, asks you to teach his son philosophy. The fee is enormous and the neighbors are watching.

choices.label: Take the son as a student
choices.resultText: The boy is bright and frightened. Syracuse's factor notes who teaches him. Your neighbors note the silver.

choices.label: Refuse; you teach citizens
choices.resultText: The tyrant hires a sophist. Syracuse's factor sends you a jar of oil, unexplained.

scene: Your students have written a comedy for the Dionysia in which a philosopher, recognizably you, sells wisdom by the jar. They want your blessing.

choices.label: Bless it and sit in the front row
choices.resultText: The theatre roars. You laugh at the jar. Students who see you laugh at yourself learn something no lecture teaches.

choices.label: Forbid it
choices.resultText: They stage it anyway with a fake beard. The theatre roars louder for the beard.

scene: A long winter night, a fresh scroll of Aristotle on the soul, and a symposium at a Kleitos house you had promised to attend.

choices.label: The scroll
choices.resultText: Dawn, and the whole thing read twice. The Kleitos is offended for a week. Aristotle is not.

choices.label: The symposium
choices.resultText: Good wine, a good argument with a shipwright about whether a hull has a soul. The scroll waits, unoffended.

scene: A pamphlet naming your school a nest of atheists is being read at the barbers'. Three fathers have withdrawn their sons by noon.

choices.label: Sue the author for slander
choices.resultText: The suit costs a season's fees and wins a fine you never collect. The fathers come back slowly, and the pamphlet is quoted forever.

choices.label: Let it pass
choices.resultText: It passes. The three sons do not come back. Their fathers tell other fathers why.

scene: Twenty years of scrolls by lamplight. The letters swim now, and the physician offers a cure of Egyptian salves and a month without reading.

choices.label: Pay for the cure and the month
choices.resultText: Salves, darkness, a month of dictation. The eyes come back, mostly. The month is gone entirely.

choices.label: Read on, and let the eyes go
choices.resultText: You finish the treatise. You cannot read your own hand by winter. Your students read to you, and get things wrong.
